sourceLine: Software solutions to RAW and control hazards, and register renaming as the removal of WAW and WAR: Sarangi chapter 10, sections 10.5.1, 10.5.2 and 10.11.4 (English, read in full). Compiler scheduling, delay slots and renaming listed as remedies: DSWallah Learn 'Pipeline Hazards & Stalls', romanised Hindi, translated (read in part).
title: Software Fixes: Scheduling and Register Renaming
unit: Instruction Pipelining: Hazards, Stalls and Fixes
quickIdea: The compiler can move an independent instruction into the gap a hazard would leave, and the hardware or the compiler can rename registers so that two instructions which merely reuse a name no longer collide. Both reduce stalls without changing what the program computes.
remember: Instruction scheduling reorders independent instructions to cover latency - the load-use gap, or the branch delay slots - and needs no hardware change.
Register renaming maps the architectural registers onto a larger set of physical registers, so a later write goes to a different physical register and WAR and WAW disappear.
Renaming removes false dependences only. A true dependence, RAW, survives renaming because the value really is needed.
Renaming is the standard answer to 'what handles certain kinds of hazards' (GATE CSE 2012 Q.20, answer: to handle certain kinds of hazards).

An anti-dependence does not always stall an in-order pipeline, because the read happens in ID long before any later write reaches WB - which is why 'an anti-dependence always creates one or more stalls' is false (GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.47).

example.prompt: For I1: ADD R1, R2, R3; I2: MUL R7, R1, R3; I3: SUB R4, R1, R5; I4: ADD R3, R2, R4; I5: MUL R7, R8, R9, decide whether S1 (anti-dependence between I2 and I5), S2 (anti-dependence between I2 and I4) and S3 (an anti-dependence always creates one or more stalls) hold.
example.work: I2 reads R1 and R3 and writes R7; I5 writes R7 and reads R8 and R9, so I2 to I5 is write-after-write, an output dependence, not anti. I2 reads R3 and I4 writes R3, so I2 to I4 is write-after-read: an anti-dependence, true. S3 fails on two counts: in an in-order pipeline the read in ID precedes any later write in WB, and renaming removes the dependence altogether.
example.answer: Only S2 is true, the accepted answer of GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.47.

gateAngle: GATE asks this in two ways: a definition question about what renaming is for (2012 Q.20) and a statement question where the word 'always' is the trap (2015 Set 3 Q.47). The reasoning is the same: decide whether the pair is RAW, WAR or WAW, then ask whether that kind of dependence can hurt this pipeline.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A compiler cannot fill the gap after a load because no independent instruction is available. What else can it do, and what does that cost?
variations.why: It shows scheduling is one of a family of fixes, and that the fallback is the hardware stall.
variations.answer: It can rename registers or reschedule a different block, but if nothing independent exists the load-use bubble remains: the processor inserts it. The cost is one cycle of throughput per occurrence, exactly the stall the hardware would have produced without any scheduling attempt.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does renaming not help a RAW hazard?
variations.why: It is the boundary between removing a name collision and removing a real dependence.
variations.answer: Because the second instruction needs the value the first produces. Renaming gives the writer a new physical register but the reader still has to read that same new register, so the dependence is carried along with the renaming rather than dissolved by it.

trap.what: Thinking renaming removes stalls caused by true dependences.
trap.why: Renaming acts on the names, and a true dependence is about the value. A pipeline still waits for the producer of a value it needs.
trap.counterexample: LOAD R1, [A]; ADD R2, R1, R3 with every register renamed: the pair still needs its one bubble, because the loaded word is not available at the start of the consumer's EX cycle.

check.question: Two instructions write the same register in program order. Name the dependence, say whether it stalls an in-order pipeline, and say what removes it in an out-of-order one.
check.answer: WAW, an output dependence; it does not stall an in-order pipeline; register renaming removes it out of order.
check.explanation: In order, the first write completes before the second begins, so the final value is correct; out of order the second could finish first, and renaming gives each write its own physical register.
